agenda: The situation in the Middle East Letter dated 26 January 2018 from the Panel of Experts on Yemen mandated by Security Council resolution 2342 (2017) addressed to the President of the Security Council (S/2018/68)
penholder: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.by: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
steps.intent: The United Kingdom’s objective is to renew the Yemen sanctions regime and the Panel of Experts’ mandate while reinforcing implementation of the arms embargo, humanitarian access and the UN-led political process. The main difficulty will be balancing robust language on Houthi attacks and arms-embargo violations with the need to retain Russian and Chinese support, so the draft avoids naming Iran while leaving room for further designations. It is designed as a credible penholder text that can secure at least nine votes and avoid a veto.

messages.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia supports renewing the Panel's mandate and pursuing a Yemeni-led political settlement, but the current text is unbalanced in its condemnation of attacks. We ask the penholder to condemn attacks on civilians by all parties, including Saudi-led coalition airstrikes, and to call explicitly for lifting restrictions that block humanitarian and commercial imports. We also seek a humanitarian carve-out for any additional designations.
messages.China: China supports the current draft and the renewal of the sanctions measures and the Panel of Experts mandate. We welcome the emphasis on a Yemeni-led political process and on rapid, safe and unhindered humanitarian access. We encourage all parties to engage with Special Envoy Griffiths and to comply with international humanitarian law. China will vote in favour.
messages.Côte d’Ivoire: Côte d’Ivoire supports the draft as presented. We welcome its emphasis on Yemen’s sovereignty and unity, the need for a Yemeni-led political process, and rapid, safe and unhindered humanitarian access. We also support renewal of the sanctions and Panel mandate and call on all parties and Member States to cooperate fully with the Panel. We encourage the penholder to maintain broad consensus as negotiations continue.
messages.Equatorial Guinea: Equatorial Guinea supports the renewal of the sanctions measures and the Panel of Experts mandate, and appreciates the draft's focus on Yemen's sovereignty, humanitarian access and a Yemeni-led political process. We encourage all parties to engage constructively with the Special Envoy and to facilitate unimpeded humanitarian assistance. We can support the text as drafted.
messages.Ethiopia: Ethiopia supports the draft as a balanced basis for renewing the sanctions and the Panel of Experts mandate. We welcome its emphasis on Yemeni sovereignty, humanitarian access and the UN-led political process under the Special Envoy. We have no changes to request at this stage.
messages.France: France supports the renewal of the sanctions measures and the Panel of Experts mandate. We ask the penholder to strengthen the humanitarian-access paragraph by referring explicitly to commercial imports and access to ports and airports, and to add accountability language. These changes are important for France and would allow us to support the text.
messages.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan supports the draft as circulated by the United Kingdom and has no amendments to request at this stage. We welcome the renewal of the sanctions measures and the Panel of Experts mandate, and we stress the importance of a Yemeni-led political settlement, unimpeded humanitarian access, and full respect for Yemen's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity.
messages.Kuwait: Kuwait supports the UK draft and welcomes its firm condemnation of Houthi missile attacks and the renewal of sanctions and the Panel of Experts. We request that OP2 explicitly reaffirm support for the legitimate Government of Yemen under President Hadi, consistent with resolution 2216 (2015). We also ask that OP3 mention fuel, food and medical supplies through all ports and across frontlines, and that OP4 condemn attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure by any party.
messages.Netherlands: Netherlands supports renewal of the sanctions and Panel mandate, but the Council’s message must apply IHL and civilian-protection obligations to all parties. Please broaden OP4 beyond Houthi attacks and add a new operative paragraph requiring all parties to protect civilians and humanitarian access and report on impediments. We can otherwise support the text with minor technical edits.
messages.Peru: Peru supports renewing the Panel of Experts and the sanctions measures, as well as the draft’s political and humanitarian orientation. We ask the penholder to reflect the need for accountability and to strengthen protections for medical and humanitarian personnel and civilian objects in OP4; with these adjustments Peru can join consensus.
messages.Poland: Poland supports the draft as circulated and is ready to join consensus. We welcome its focus on humanitarian access, protection of civilians, support for the Special Envoy's political process, and full implementation of the arms embargo and sanctions regime.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports renewal of the sanctions and the Panel of Experts mandate, but the text must be balanced and not single out one party. We ask the penholder to condemn all attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure by all parties, including Saudi-led coalition airstrikes, and to call for lifting restrictions on commercial and humanitarian access through all Yemeni ports. Sanctions language should remain within existing criteria and not be used for political pressure.
messages.Sweden: Sweden supports renewal of the sanctions regime and the Panel of Experts mandate and thanks the UK for the draft. We ask that OP4 be rebalanced to condemn attacks on civilians and IHL violations by all parties, not only Houthi attacks. We also request a WPS reference in OP1 and a new accountability paragraph covering sexual and gender-based violence and child recruitment.
messages.United States of America: The United States supports the draft as written. It strongly condemns Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and vessels, reaffirms the arms embargo, and backs the Special Envoy's political process. We urge the Council to adopt it without delay.

steps.summary: The revised draft broadens civilian-protection and humanitarian-access language and adds WPS and accountability provisions while retaining specific condemnation of Houthi missile attacks, the arms embargo, and support for the legitimate Government. It avoids explicitly naming Saudi-led coalition airstrikes, preserving key UK and US equities, while accommodating enough requests to sustain Council consensus.

messages.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia appreciates the penholder's partial acceptance and remains ready to support the renewal of the sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate. However, the text still does not explicitly name Saudi-led coalition airstrikes that have caused civilian casualties, and it only urges facilitation rather than lifting restrictions on imports. Bolivia therefore asks that PP7/OP4 include coalition airstrikes and that OP3 call for the immediate lifting of land, air and sea restrictions; these points are important for our support.
messages.China: China supports the current draft and appreciates the penholder’s efforts to accommodate Council concerns. The text reaffirms Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, supports a Yemeni-led political process, and calls for unhindered humanitarian access, which are China’s key priorities. We encourage all parties to engage with Special Envoy Griffiths and to comply fully with the arms embargo. China will join consensus and vote in favour of the draft.
messages.Côte d’Ivoire: Côte d'Ivoire supports the current text as a balanced renewal of the sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate. We welcome the emphasis on unimpeded humanitarian access, protection of civilians, accountability, and a Yemeni-led political process under the Special Envoy. We encourage the Council to maintain unity and adopt the draft by consensus.
messages.Equatorial Guinea: Equatorial Guinea supports the current draft, which balances humanitarian concerns with respect for Yemen's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity. We welcome the focus on unimpeded humanitarian access and the renewal of the Panel of Experts, and we are prepared to vote in favour.
messages.Ethiopia: Ethiopia supports the current draft and thanks the penholder for its balanced text. We welcome the emphasis on humanitarian access, civilian protection, and a Yemeni-led political process under the Special Envoy. Ethiopia will vote in favour and urges all parties to cooperate fully with the Panel of Experts and to implement resolution 2216 (2015).
messages.France: France supports the draft as revised and welcomes the incorporation of our earlier points on humanitarian access, commercial imports, port and airport access, and accountability. We remain fully supportive of the Special Envoy's efforts and call on all parties to engage in good faith with the political process. France is ready to join consensus on this text.
messages.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan supports the draft as presently worded. It reflects the Council’s concern over the humanitarian situation, the need for unimpeded humanitarian access, full implementation of the arms embargo and renewal of the Panel’s mandate, while reaffirming Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity. We encourage the Council to maintain consensus and proceed to a vote on this text.
messages.Kuwait: Kuwait supports the current text and has no further changes. The incorporation of support for the legitimate Government, humanitarian access, and all-party condemnation addresses our priorities. We encourage the Council to move to a vote and call on all parties to cooperate with the Panel of Experts and the Special Envoy.
messages.Netherlands: The Netherlands thanks the United Kingdom for revising the text and welcomes the incorporation of our proposals on humanitarian access through Hodeidah and Sana'a airport, civilian-protection reporting and balanced condemnation of attacks. We support the current draft and would prefer no further substantive changes so that the Council can speak with one voice. We encourage swift adoption and full implementation, particularly on humanitarian access, accountability and the arms embargo.
messages.Peru: Peru supports the revised draft. Our earlier concerns on accountability and on the protection of humanitarian and medical personnel have been incorporated, and the text maintains a balanced emphasis on the political process, humanitarian access and full implementation of the arms embargo. We can support the text as presented and encourage the Council to speak with one voice.
messages.Poland: Poland supports the draft as a balanced renewal of the Yemen sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate. We welcome its strong language on humanitarian access, protection of civilians, accountability and full implementation of the arms embargo. Poland encourages all Council members to unite behind the text and remains ready to work with the penholder on follow-up reporting.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports the renewal of the sanctions regime and the Panel's mandate, and welcomes the partial incorporation of our proposals on humanitarian access and designation criteria. However, the text remains unbalanced: it names only Houthi attacks while omitting Saudi-led coalition airstrikes that have caused civilian casualties. We also ask that OP3 explicitly cover all Yemeni ports to ensure unhindered commercial and humanitarian access. With these changes, we are ready to support the draft.
messages.Sweden: Sweden thanks the penholder for incorporating our priorities on women's full and equal participation, all-party condemnation of attacks on civilians, and accountability for sexual and gender-based violence and child recruitment. We support the revised draft as a balanced compromise and have no further requests; we urge the Council to adopt it without delay.
messages.United States of America: The United States supports the current text as a balanced renewal of the Yemen sanctions regime and the Panel of Experts mandate. We welcome the clear condemnation of Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia and the retention of the arms embargo, while noting the important humanitarian access provisions. We encourage all Council members to join consensus and adopt the resolution without delay.

reasons.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia’s key concern on condemning coalition airstrikes was substantially reflected, and while its request for immediate lifting of all restrictions was not fully accepted, the compromise on humanitarian access was sufficient for it to support the renewal and use the statement to press its humanitarian and sovereignty concerns.
reasons.China: China generally supports Security Council unity on Yemen, humanitarian access, and a political settlement while avoiding confrontation with major stakeholders. The draft is balanced enough and China had already indicated support, so it votes yes.
reasons.Côte d’Ivoire: Côte d’Ivoire had already indicated support for the draft, made no additional requests, and the penholder accepted the outcome. Voting in favour is consistent with its support for Council unity on Yemen, humanitarian access, and a Yemeni-led political process.
reasons.Equatorial Guinea: Equatorial Guinea supported the draft in the final negotiating round without outstanding requests, and it has a general interest in renewing the Yemen sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate while backing humanitarian access and a political settlement.
reasons.Ethiopia: Ethiopia had already signaled support with no requested changes, and the resolution aligns with its preference for UN-led diplomacy, regional stability, and humanitarian access. A yes vote is consistent with its Council posture.
reasons.France: France had already supported the draft with no requests, and the text aligns with French priorities on humanitarian access, protection of civilians, accountability, and renewal of the sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate. Voting yes is consistent with France’s Council position and its support for a political process led by the UN Special Envoy.
reasons.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan had already indicated support for the draft and made no specific requests, and the text aligns with its stated support for UN mediation, sovereignty, humanitarian access and Council unity. A yes vote is consistent with its role as an elected member seeking a balanced but firm Council response.
reasons.Kuwait: Kuwait supported the UK draft in the final negotiation round without requesting changes and, as a GCC member, backs renewal of the Yemen sanctions/Panel mandate alongside the resolution’s humanitarian and political messages.
reasons.Netherlands: The Netherlands supports renewing the Yemen sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate and backs the draft’s humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and accountability provisions, consistent with its multilateral and human-rights priorities.
reasons.Peru: Peru supported the draft in the last negotiation round and raised no outstanding requests, so it would vote in favour. With no particular need to explain its vote, Peru would likely join the consensus without taking the floor.
reasons.Poland: Poland supports the UK draft because it renews the Yemen sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate while pressing for humanitarian access, civilian protection and a UN-led political process. This aligns with Poland’s indicated support in the final negotiation round and its broader commitment to international humanitarian law.
reasons.Russian Federation: The draft is a routine renewal of the Yemen sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate and incorporates enough of Russia’s proposed balanced language on coalition airstrikes and port access; Moscow has no grounds to abstain or veto and need not take the floor before the vote.
reasons.Sweden: Sweden supports the draft because it advances humanitarian access, civilian protection, accountability, women’s participation, and implementation of the arms embargo and sanctions, consistent with Sweden’s established foreign policy priorities. The text also backs the UN-led political process and renews essential monitoring mandates.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: As the sponsor and a permanent member, the United Kingdom would vote in favour of a text reflecting its policy priorities on humanitarian access, civilian protection, accountability, UN-led mediation, and renewal of the sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate. There is no reason for the UK to abstain or veto its own draft.
reasons.United States of America: The resolution renews the Yemen sanctions and Panel of Experts mandate, supports the UN-led political process, and presses for humanitarian access and accountability, aligning with U.S. interests and avoiding a veto confrontation. A yes vote is consistent with the U.S. approach to the Saudi-led coalition, the legitimate Yemeni government, and countering Houthi attacks while supporting a balanced text.

before.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia (Plurinational State of) will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We do so because the text recognizes the severity of the humanitarian catastrophe in Yemen and, as we insisted during negotiations, condemns all attacks against civilians and civilian objects, including airstrikes by the Saudi-led coalition that have caused civilian casualties. We regret that the text does not go as far as we proposed in calling for the immediate lifting of all land, air and sea restrictions, but we welcome the calls to remove unnecessary restrictions and to facilitate access through Hudaydah port, Sana’a airport and all Yemeni ports. Bolivia reaffirms the need to respect Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, to ensure rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access, to implement the arms embargo fully and without politicization, and to support a genuine Yemeni-led political process. The humanitarian dimension must remain central and must never be used as a pretext for further militarization or external interference.
before.China: China supports the draft resolution. We believe that the crisis in Yemen can only be resolved through an inclusive Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process. The humanitarian situation is grave, and all parties must facilitate safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access and comply with international humanitarian law. China also stresses the importance of respecting Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity and calls on all parties to engage constructively with the Special Envoy. China will vote in favour of the draft resolution.
before.Ethiopia: Ethiopia votes in favour of the draft resolution. We support the renewal of the Panel of Experts and the sanctions measures as a means of reinforcing the political process and upholding the arms embargo. We emphasize the need for full respect for Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, and we call on all parties to ensure rapid, safe and unhindered humanitarian access and to engage constructively with the Special Envoy towards a comprehensive political settlement.
before.France: Mr President, France votes in favour of this resolution. It renews the sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts and sends a clear message on the humanitarian emergency in Yemen: all parties must ensure rapid, safe and unimpeded humanitarian access, protect civilians and humanitarian personnel, comply with international humanitarian law and fully implement the arms embargo. France strongly supports the efforts of Special Envoy Martin Griffiths and calls on all parties to engage without preconditions and in good faith towards an inclusive political settlement. We reiterate that attacks against civilians by any party, including Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia and airstrikes causing civilian casualties, must cease, and that those responsible for violations must be held accountable.
before.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan votes in favour of this draft resolution. We support the renewal of the mandate of the Panel of Experts and the sanctions measures, which are important for upholding the arms embargo and for the Council’s ability to follow developments in Yemen objectively. Kazakhstan remains deeply concerned by the humanitarian situation, including the risk of famine, cholera and the obstruction of relief supplies, and we call on all parties to ensure rapid, safe and unhindered humanitarian access. We also support the central role of the United Nations Special Envoy and a Yemeni-led political process aimed at a comprehensive settlement. At the same time, Kazakhstan stresses the importance of respecting Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, and we urge all parties to comply with international humanitarian law and to protect civilians. We believe this resolution is balanced, supports accountability and keeps the Council engaged in the search for peace.
before.Sweden: Sweden votes in favour of this resolution. We welcome the Council’s clear message on the protection of civilians, unimpeded humanitarian access, accountability for violations of international humanitarian and human rights law, including sexual and gender-based violence and the recruitment of children, and the full and equal participation of women in the political process. We also support the renewal of the Panel of Experts and the sanctions measures, and we call on all parties and all Member States to implement them fully. The humanitarian crisis in Yemen demands that this Council speak with one voice and that today’s commitments be translated without delay into action on the ground.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom will vote in favour of this resolution, which we have tabled, because it responds to the grave humanitarian and security situation in Yemen. It affirms support for a Yemeni-led political process under Special Envoy Martin Griffiths, insists on rapid, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, condemns attacks on civilians by all parties, and underscores the obligation on all Member States to implement the arms embargo. We urge all parties to engage in good faith, comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and humanitarian workers, and cooperate with the Panel of Experts. The Council must speak clearly and remain seized of this matter.
before.United States of America: The United States supports this resolution. It renews the sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts at a critical moment, and it makes clear that all parties must respect international humanitarian law, protect civilians, and allow rapid, safe and unimpeded humanitarian access. We thank the United Kingdom for its work. The United States remains committed to Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, to support for the legitimate Government of Yemen, and to a comprehensive political settlement under United Nations auspices. We call on all parties, including the Houthis, to cease attacks, engage with Special Envoy Martin Griffiths, and comply fully with the arms embargo. The United States will vote in favor.

after.Côte d’Ivoire:
Mr. President,

Côte d’Ivoire voted in favour of the resolution just adopted. We did so because the humanitarian catastrophe in Yemen demands that this Council act with a single voice, and because we support the renewal of the Panel of Experts and the sanctions regime established by resolution 2216 (2015). The Panel’s work remains essential for upholding the arms embargo and for ensuring accountability for violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law.

Côte d’Ivoire calls on all parties to facilitate rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access to all affected areas, including through the port of Hodeidah and Sana’a airport, and to remove all bureaucratic impediments to the delivery of food, fuel and medicines. We condemn all attacks against civilians and civilian objects, by any party, and stress the obligation of all parties to respect international humanitarian law and to protect humanitarian personnel, facilities and assets.

We reaffirm our commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Yemen and to a Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under the auspices of the Special Envoy, Mr. Martin Griffiths. Côte d’Ivoire urges all parties to engage constructively, without preconditions and in good faith, and calls on all Member States to implement fully the arms embargo and to cooperate with the Panel of Experts. The people of Yemen deserve peace, dignity and hope, and this Council must remain fully engaged in supporting them.
after.Kuwait:
Mr. President,

Kuwait voted in favour of this resolution because it responds to the grave humanitarian situation in Yemen and reaffirms the need for a political settlement based on the Gulf Cooperation Council initiative, the outcomes of the National Dialogue Conference and resolution 2216 (2015). We support Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity and the legitimate Government of Yemen under President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi. We welcome the Council’s clear call for rapid, safe and unhindered humanitarian access through all Yemeni ports, including Hudaydah, and Sana’a airport, and for the removal of unnecessary restrictions on commercial and humanitarian imports. Kuwait also welcomes the condemnation of Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia and stresses the obligation of all Member States to implement the arms embargo fully so that weapons do not reach the Houthis. At the same time, all parties must respect international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and facilitate relief work. Kuwait remains committed to supporting the efforts of Special Envoy Martin Griffiths and to assisting the brotherly Yemeni people. We call on all parties to engage constructively and without preconditions to end the suffering of the Yemeni people.
after.Netherlands:
Mr President,

The Netherlands voted in favour of this resolution. We welcome its unanimous adoption, which sends a clear signal that the Security Council remains seized of the situation in Yemen and that the humanitarian catastrophe and the threat to international peace and security cannot be ignored. We thank the United Kingdom for its leadership as penholder.

We strongly support the renewal of the sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts, and we call on all Member States to implement the arms embargo fully and effectively. The Netherlands also welcomes the resolution’s clear condemnation of attacks against civilians and civilian objects by all parties, including Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia and Saudi-led coalition airstrikes that have caused civilian casualties. International humanitarian law applies to all parties without exception.

The humanitarian situation remains dire. We urge all parties to facilitate rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access, including through the port of Hodeidah and Sana’a airport, and to protect humanitarian personnel and civilian infrastructure such as schools, hospitals and water facilities. We also stress the need for accountability for violations and abuses, including sexual and gender-based violence and the recruitment and use of children.

The Netherlands fully supports Special Envoy Martin Griffiths and a Yemeni-led, inclusive political process with the full and meaningful participation of women. The Council’s words must now be translated into action on the ground.
after.Peru:
Mr President,
Peru voted in favour of this resolution. We welcome its adoption and thank the United Kingdom for its efforts. The humanitarian situation in Yemen is among the most grave in the world, and this Council cannot remain indifferent to the risk of famine, cholera, displacement and restrictions on life-saving assistance. We therefore reiterate that all parties must comply with international humanitarian and human rights law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and ensure rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access to all affected areas, including through Hodeidah port, Sana’a airport and across frontlines.
Peru also stresses the need for full implementation of the arms embargo and for cooperation with the Panel of Experts. At the same time, we reaffirm our support for Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity and for a Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under United Nations auspices and the Special Envoy. Peru calls on all parties to engage in good faith, cease hostilities, take confidence-building measures, and work towards an inclusive political settlement with the full and equal participation of women. Peru will continue to follow the situation closely and to support the Council’s efforts.
after.Poland:
Mr President, Poland voted in favour of this resolution because the Security Council must speak clearly and with one voice in the face of the humanitarian catastrophe and continued instability in Yemen. We welcome its unanimous adoption.

Poland strongly supports Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity. We reaffirm our support for a Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under the auspices of the United Nations and for the efforts of Special Envoy Martin Griffiths. All parties must engage in good faith, without preconditions, and in an inclusive manner, including with the full and equal participation of women.

The humanitarian situation requires urgent action. All parties must facilitate rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access to all affected areas, including through the port of Hudaydah and Sana’a airport, and must protect civilians, humanitarian personnel and civilian infrastructure. Poland condemns all attacks against civilians and civilian objects by any party, including Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia and airstrikes that cause civilian casualties. Those responsible for violations of international humanitarian law and human rights law must be held accountable.

We also stress the importance of full implementation of the arms embargo and the sanctions measures renewed by this resolution. Poland will continue to support the work of the Panel of Experts and the Council’s efforts to advance a peaceful and comprehensive settlement in Yemen.
after.Russian Federation:
Mr President,
The Russian Federation voted in favour of the resolution just adopted. We share the grave concern of the international community at the continued deterioration of the humanitarian situation in Yemen, including the risk of famine, the cholera outbreak and the suffering of civilians. We are convinced that the crisis in Yemen can be resolved only through an inclusive, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under United Nations auspices. We support the efforts of Special Envoy Martin Griffiths and call on all parties to engage with him constructively, in good faith and without preconditions. We also stress the need for rapid, safe, unimpeded and sustained humanitarian access to all affected areas, including through the port of Hodeidah and Sana’a airport, and for the removal of unnecessary impediments to commercial and humanitarian supplies. The Russian Federation consistently advocates respect for the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Yemen and the need to avoid external interference in its internal affairs. We note that the resolution contains a balanced condemnation of attacks against civilians by all parties and does not contain unsubstantiated accusations against individual States. We support the renewal of the sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts, and we emphasize that they must act strictly within their mandate and avoid politicization. We call on all Member States to implement fully the arms embargo imposed by resolution 2216 (2015). The Russian Federation will continue to contribute actively to international efforts aimed at a comprehensive political settlement in Yemen.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: Thank you, Mr President. The United Kingdom welcomes the unanimous adoption of this resolution. We thank Council members for their constructive engagement and for the clear message this Council has sent on the humanitarian and security situation in Yemen. The test now is implementation. We call on all parties to engage in good faith with Special Envoy Martin Griffiths and to move towards an inclusive, Yemeni-led political settlement; to facilitate rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access, including through the port of Hodeidah and Sana’a airport; to protect civilians and humanitarian personnel; and to comply fully with international humanitarian law. We also call on all Member States to implement the arms embargo fully and to cooperate with the Panel of Experts. The United Kingdom remains committed to Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, and we will continue to support the Council in remaining seized of this matter.
